text: Displacement, and how a metal gets out of its ore

md: Stand a strip of zinc in blue copper sulfate solution and within minutes the blue drains away and the zinc turns brown. Nothing was added and nothing was heated: the two metals simply swapped places. That one swap explains how almost every metal you own was got out of the ground.

md: A metal reacts by giving its outer electrons away. In a salt solution the metal is already an ion; the metal you drop in still has its electrons. If the newcomer gives them up more readily, the two change roles. So: **a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.**

title: Why the blue fades
md: The blue belongs to the copper(II) ions in the water, not to the water. As those ions take electrons and become copper metal, the blue has nothing left to belong to — and zinc sulfate solution is colourless. The fading blue and the brown coating are one event, not two.

prompt: A more reactive metal ______ a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.
explain: Displaces. Hold on to that word — a question that asks for the type of reaction wants *displacement*, not a description of the colour change.

md:
Testing every metal against every salt solution gives a grid, and the grid gives you the order without knowing any of it in advance. Read **along a row**: the metal that reacts with the most solutions is the most reactive. Read **down a column** and you see the mirror image — the metals that can displace that one.
Here magnesium reacts with three solutions, zinc with two, copper with one and silver with none, so the order is magnesium, zinc, copper, silver.

prompt: Use the grid. Which metal is the least reactive of the four?
explain: Silver: its row is empty, so it cannot displace anything, and its column is full, so everything can displace it.

md:
**The question.** Zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Write the word equation and then the balanced symbol equation.
**Step 1 — decide whether it reacts.** Zinc is above copper, so it does.
**Step 2 — swap the metals, keep the rest.** The sulfate is a spectator: it belongs to the copper at the start and to the zinc at the end. In words: zinc + copper(II) sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper.

prompt: Try the same swap: magnesium + copper(II) sulfate → magnesium sulfate + ______
explain: Copper. Magnesium takes the sulfate and the copper is pushed out as the metal, exactly as the zinc did.

md:
**Step 3 — put in the formulae.** $\ce{Zn}$, $\ce{CuSO4}$, $\ce{ZnSO4}$, $\ce{Cu}$. Write all four before balancing anything.
**Step 4 — balance and check.** One zinc, one copper and one sulfate on each side already, so no numbers are needed: $\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}$. Capital letters matter here — Cu is copper, CU is nothing.

prompt: Which of these is the balanced symbol equation for magnesium in copper(II) sulfate solution?
explain: The sulfate group stays whole and moves across as one piece. Splitting it up, or inventing a metal-to-metal compound, changes the chemistry rather than balancing it.

md:
The same idea works with a solid oxide instead of a solution. Aluminium is above iron, so aluminium takes iron's oxygen:
$\ce{2Al + Fe2O3 -> 2Fe + Al2O3}$.
So much energy is released that the iron comes out **molten**, which is why this reaction is used to weld railway track in place, out on the line.

alt: A thermite mixture burning in a small crucible on a metal stand at night, throwing a brilliant white flare and a shower of orange sparks, with white smoke rising above it
caption: A thermite charge part-way through reacting. A diagram cannot show how bright it is, and the brightness is the evidence for the energy released.
prompt: Name the two reactants and the two products. Which element is losing oxygen and which is gaining it? What does the brightness tell you about the energy change?
Why does the aluminium take the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide?
options: aluminium is more reactive than iron
aluminium melts at a lower temperature
the aluminium powder has a large surface area
answer: aluminium is more reactive than iron
explain: Position in the series decides what can happen; surface area only decides how fast it happens once it can.

md:
Almost every metal is found in the ground **combined**, usually as an oxide, because the compound is more stable than the metal. A rock with enough of that compound in it to be worth digging up is called an **ore**: haematite for iron, bauxite for aluminium.
Extracting the metal means taking the oxygen off, and how you do it depends on where the metal sits. Carbon is the deciding line: it can pull oxygen off a metal **below** it, but not off one **above** it.

prompt: A rock with enough of a metal compound in it to be worth extracting is called an ______.
explain: An ore. Keep the two names apart: haematite is the ore of iron, bauxite the ore of aluminium.

md:
**Above carbon** — potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium — the metal holds its oxygen too tightly for carbon, so it is extracted by **electrolysis**, which is expensive because of the electricity it needs.
**Below carbon** — zinc, iron, copper — the ore is **reduced by carbon**: heat it with coke and the carbon takes the oxygen away, leaving the metal. That is why iron is cheap and aluminium is not.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Extraction of Metals"
why: The link from a metal's position in the series to the method used on it, in one short run.

prompt: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon. Why?
options: aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take its oxygen
electrolysis is the cheaper of the two methods
aluminium oxide does not contain any oxygen
answer: aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take its oxygen
explain: Electrolysis is in fact far more expensive, which is exactly why it is kept for the metals carbon cannot reach.

Say why aluminium needs electrolysis and iron does not.

Displacement usually sits inside Question 1 as a **results grid**: four metals, four solutions, and two or three marks for reading an order out of it. Then a word equation at **[1]-[2]**, a symbol equation marked in three parts, and a colour. Extraction comes either as a one-line reason or inside the 6-mark writing question. When the command word is *Name*, the answer is the single word **displacement**.
